Canonical Tag Checker

Fetches a URL you choose for real, reads its canonical link tag(s), and -- when there is exactly one -- fetches that URL too, then classifies the evidence into named canonicalization misconfiguration patterns: multiple conflicting canonical tags, a relative or cross-domain canonical, a protocol mismatch, and a canonical target that is unreachable, redirects, or is itself marked noindex.

1. Run the CLI against your page

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node cli/check.mjs https://example.com/some/page --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the page's URL, and (when relevant) the one canonical URL it names; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

What was fetched

FetchURLStatusRedirects

Common questions

What does a canonical tag actually do?

A link tag with rel=canonical and an href in a page's head tells search engines which URL is the authoritative version of this content, so duplicate or near-duplicate URLs (with tracking parameters, alternate sort orders, http vs https, www vs no-www) consolidate their ranking signal onto one page instead of splitting it.

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

Reading another origin's response headers and body from inside a browser tab is CORS-gated, and most sites set no Access-Control-Allow-Origin at all -- so a page running in your browser cannot reliably fetch an arbitrary URL and read what came back, even a URL you own. Only a non-browser HTTP client, like the CLI here (or curl), can do that. Run the CLI, then paste its JSON output here for a rendered report.

Why does it sometimes make a second request?

When the page names exactly one canonical URL that differs from the page you fetched, the tool follows it -- the same way a search engine would -- to check the canonical target actually resolves, does not redirect further, and is not itself marked noindex. A canonical is only useful if the page it points at is a real, indexable page.

Is a cross-domain canonical always wrong?

No -- it is a real, supported pattern for syndicated content, where a republished article points its canonical back at the original source. It is flagged as a notice worth checking because it is also exactly what a hardcoded staging URL or a copy-pasted template leaves behind, and either mistake silently tells search engines to index a different site's page instead of yours.

Does a clean report mean the page has no SEO issues?

No. This checks canonical-tag evidence from one or two real fetches -- it is not a full SEO audit, does not crawl your whole site, and cannot see an issue outside what a canonical tag and its target page can show. Treat a clean report as evidence about this specific page's canonicalization, not a determination that the page or site has no other SEO problems.

Already running a full-site crawl? See how this checker compares to Screaming Frog SEO Spider — a one-URL CI gate next to a whole-site crawler, and when each one is the right tool. Only checking one page yourself? See how this compares to reading a canonical tag in view-source — the difference is whether anyone fetches the page the tag points at.

Seeing a "danger" finding on a page with a tag on it, not a missing one? See why two canonical tags is worse than none — a plugin and a template can both emit one, and only the first is ever honored. Got a report back with several findings at once? See which one to fix first.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks canonical-tag evidence from one or two real fetches. A clean report describes what these fetches found, not a guarantee the page has no other SEO issues.

vs-checking-canonicals-by-view-source.ht.text:
← Canonical Tag Checker

Canonical Tag Checker vs. checking canonicals by view-source

View-source needs no tool beyond what is already open: right-click, view page source (or the Elements panel), and read the <head>. It is exact about the one page you have open -- whether a canonical tag exists, whether its href is absolute, whether it points at the right domain. It tells you nothing about the page that tag points at, because checking that means fetching a second URL, and view-source only ever shows you the page you already loaded.

Page checkedIts canonical tagview-source showsThis tool shows
/old-guide/<link rel=canonical href="https://example.com/guide/">One absolute, same-domain canonical tag — nothing wrong with itSame tag, plus: the target it names is itself marked noindex

Viewed in view-source, /old-guide/'s canonical tag has nothing wrong with it: one tag, absolute URL, same domain, same protocol. Every check you could run against that markup alone passes. This tool fetches /guide/ too — the page the canonical actually names — and reads what it says about itself. In the worked example below, /guide/ carries a noindex meta robots tag. The canonical on /old-guide/ is the instruction "index /guide/ instead of me"; the target page is saying "do not index me." Neither page, read alone, shows that contradiction — the practical effect is usually that neither page ends up indexed at all.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Does this one page have a canonical tag, and does it look sane on its face?Either method answers this correctly; view-source is the faster route for a single, familiar page.
Does the URL that canonical points at actually resolve, and is it marked indexable?This tool — it makes the second fetch for you and reads the target's status code and meta robots. view-source has no way to follow a link to a different URL.
I just want to confirm a typo-free canonical href on a page I'm actively editing.view-source — no need to leave the editor for a one-off spot check with no target-page question attached.
I migrated a batch of URLs and want to confirm none of the new canonical targets are accidentally noindexed.This tool — checking each target by hand means opening every one in a second tab and reading its meta robots yourself, for every URL in the batch.

This tool needs no account: it is a static report viewer, and the fetches happen from the zero-dependency CLI on your own machine, never through this site.

Common questions

What does checking a canonical tag by view-source get wrong?

View-source (or a browser's Elements panel) shows you the one page you already have open. It is exact about that page's own markup: whether there is a canonical tag, whether its href is absolute, whether it points at the right domain. It tells you nothing about the page the canonical points at, because that is a different URL you have not fetched -- and a canonical tag is only doing its job if the page it names is actually indexable.

Can you give a concrete example?

A migrated blog post at /old-guide/ carries one canonical tag, absolute, same domain, same protocol, naming https://example.com/guide/. Viewed in view-source, that tag has nothing wrong with it. Fetching /guide/ as well -- what this tool does automatically -- shows that page carries a noindex meta robots directive. The canonical on /old-guide/ is telling search engines "index /guide/ instead of me," and /guide/ is telling them "do not index me." Neither page, read alone, shows the contradiction.

Isn't view-source already exact about what a page contains?

About the one page you opened, yes -- it will not miss a malformed tag or a typo in the href. What it cannot do is follow a link and check what is on the other end, because that is a second HTTP request to a second URL, and a browser's view-source has no reason to make one. This tool makes that second request itself, reads the target's own meta robots and status code, and reports back whether the canonical actually resolves to something indexable.

Does this replace looking at the page at all?

No. You still choose which URL to check, and you still decide what to do about a finding -- this does not edit anything. What it removes is the step of manually opening a second tab, fetching the canonical target yourself, and reading its meta robots or status code by eye, for every page whose canonical you want to trust.

Verified against this tool's own worked example (a canonical whose target carries a noindex directive): the finding it reports is "Canonical target is itself marked noindex."

vs-screaming-frog.html.text:
Canonical Tag Checker vs. Screaming Frog SEO Spider

These solve different problems and are not in competition with each other. This checker answers one narrow question fast, for free, with no install: does this one URL's canonical tag actually check out? Screaming Frog SEO Spider answers a much bigger question: what does every URL on this site look like, across dozens of SEO signals at once?

Canonical Tag CheckerScreaming Frog SEO Spider
ScopeOne URL per runAn entire site, crawled
What it checksCanonical-tag evidence only: conflicting tags, cross-domain, protocol mismatch, and whether the canonical target itself resolves, redirects, or is noindexedDozens of SEO signals: status codes, redirects, titles, meta descriptions, hreflang, structured data, canonicals, and more
InstallNone -- a browser page, or a zero-dependency Node CLIA downloadable desktop application
Where it fitsA CI gate against one URL, or a quick check before/after a deployA periodic full-site technical SEO audit
CostFreeSee screamingfrog.co.uk for current licensing

Common questions

Is this a replacement for Screaming Frog SEO Spider?

No. Screaming Frog SEO Spider crawls an entire site and reports on dozens of SEO signals at once -- titles, meta descriptions, status codes, redirect chains, hreflang, structured data, and canonicals among them. This checker does one thing for one URL at a time: fetch it, read its canonical tag(s), and follow the canonical to check it actually resolves. It is a narrow, free, scriptable gate, not a crawler.

When should I use this instead of a full crawl?

When you want a fast, no-install answer for one URL -- checking a single page before or after a deploy, or wiring a canonical-tag regression gate into your own CI against a staging URL -- without installing desktop software or running a crawl of the whole site.

When should I use Screaming Frog instead?

When you need the whole picture: every URL on a site, cross-referenced against sitemaps, internal links, and dozens of other SEO signals at once, with a desktop UI for exploring the results. That is a fundamentally different job from checking one URL's canonical evidence, and Screaming Frog is a well-established, purpose-built tool for it.

Do the two tools check the same things?

Canonical tags are one of many checks a full Screaming Frog crawl covers. This tool covers only that one signal, in more focused depth for a single URL: it also follows the canonical to its own destination and reports whether that destination actually resolves, redirects, or is itself marked noindex -- evidence a same-page-only canonical audit would not surface.

which-canonical-finding-to-fix-first.htm.text:
← Canonical Tag Checker

Which canonical-tag finding to fix first

A report with several findings at once is not a to-do list in the order it prints them. This tool already grades each finding danger or notice — here is what that grading means in practice, and how to wire the CLI's exit code into CI without blocking a deploy over the wrong finding.

danger findings: the tag contradicts itself or points nowhere useful

FindingWhy it's danger, not notice
Multiple conflicting canonical tagsThe page's own markup names two different canonical URLs. Only the first is honoured, so whichever system emitted the second one is being silently ignored — usually two independent sources (a CMS plugin and a hand-written template tag) that don't know about each other.
Canonical target unreachableThe tag points at a URL that 404s or errors. The page is telling search engines "index this instead" and naming a dead end.
Canonical target marked noindexA direct self-contradiction: the canonical says "index this page," and that exact page says "don't index me." One of the two is wrong.

All three are worth fixing before the next deploy, in roughly this order: a broken or noindex'd target first, since the URL you're pointing at needs to actually work; conflicting tags second, since it's a build or template bug that will keep recurring until the duplicate emitter is found.

notice findings: usually real, rarely urgent

FindingWhat to do
Relative canonical URLWorks in every major browser and crawler today. Google's own guidance prefers an absolute URL since a relative one leaves the protocol and host to be inferred — fix it as ordinary hygiene, not as a repair.
Protocol mismatch (http/https)Usually a leftover from an http-to-https migration. Low urgency unless the site no longer serves the old protocol at all, in which case the canonical target itself may also be unreachable — check for that finding too.
Cross-domain canonicalNeeds a judgment call, not a default fix — see the FAQ below.
Canonical target redirectsThe canonical points at a URL that works, but isn't the final one — it 30x's somewhere else first. Pointing the tag straight at the final URL saves search engines a hop; not urgent, but a quick fix once you're already touching the template.

No canonical tag at all is a separate, lower-severity notice

Plenty of pages don't need one — a single canonical URL with no duplicate-content risk gets nothing extra from adding a tag that just points at itself. Treat a no-canonical-tag finding as a prompt to ask "does this page have a duplicate (a print view, a tracking-parameter variant, an amp version)?" rather than as a defect on its own.

Wiring the CLI into CI on the right signal

node cli/check.mjs <url> exits 1 only when a danger-severity finding is produced (or the fetch itself fails), and 0 otherwise — including when notice findings are present. That split is deliberate: gating a deploy on the exit code blocks the self-contradicting cases above without also failing a build over a relative URL or a deliberate cross-domain reference. Grep the --json output for notice-severity findings separately if you want them tracked, but keep the build gate on the exit code as shipped rather than tightening it to fail on any finding at all.

Common questions

Does a danger-severity finding mean the page is already deindexed?

Not necessarily. Severity here describes how directly the finding contradicts itself or points nowhere useful, not a confirmed ranking or indexing outcome — this tool checks two fetches, not what a search engine has already done with them. A canonical-target-noindex finding, for instance, is danger because the page's own markup says two contradictory things, which is worth fixing regardless of whether it has visibly affected indexing yet.

Should I fix every notice-severity finding before shipping?

Not on the same timeline as a danger finding. A relative canonical URL, for example, resolves correctly in every major browser and most crawlers today — fixing it is good hygiene per Google's own published guidance, not an urgent repair. Batch notice findings into ordinary cleanup work rather than treating a report with several of them as several fires.

Is a cross-domain canonical always something to fix?

No, and this is the one finding that needs a judgment call rather than a default. Syndicated content pointing back at the original publisher is a legitimate, deliberate use of a cross-domain canonical. A staging or preview hostname left in a canonical tag on the production page is the same finding shape from a copy-paste mistake, and it means production is telling search engines to index the staging copy instead. The finding itself can't tell these apart — check which one you're looking at before deciding what to do.

Should CI fail the build on any finding, or only danger ones?

The CLI's own exit code already makes this distinction for you: it exits 1 on a danger-severity finding and 0 otherwise, specifically so a CI gate can block a real self-contradiction (a broken or noindex'd canonical target, conflicting tags) without also failing routine deploys over a relative URL or an intentional cross-domain reference. Wiring a stricter gate that fails on any finding at all will make the check fire on legitimate cases and get bypassed.

Want the accuracy question instead — what this tool checks and doesn't? See the tool's own FAQ, or how it compares to a whole-site crawler and to checking canonicals by view-source.

why-two-canonical-tags-is-worse-than-non.text:
← Canonical Tag Checker

Why two canonical tags on one page is worse than none

A missing canonical tag is a notice: search engines infer a reasonable one on their own, usually the URL you requested. Two canonical tags naming different URLs on the same page is a danger: the page's own <head> is contradicting itself, and only the first tag found is ever honored -- the rest are silently ignored, by design, not as an error either side reports back to you.

A worked example

A blog post at /guide/ runs an SEO plugin that auto-generates <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/guide/"> from the page's own URL on every request. The theme's template -- written before the plugin was installed, and never removed -- also emits its own tag: <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/blog/guide/">. Fetching that page and checking it:

FindingSeverityWhat it reports
multiple-conflicting-canonical danger "2 canonical tags naming 2 different URLs" -- evidence: https://example.com/guide/ | https://example.com/blog/guide/

Which of the two wins is decided by markup order -- whichever the plugin or the template happens to print first in <head> -- not by which one anyone actually intended. Neither the plugin nor the template knows the other one already added a tag, so nothing on the page itself ever surfaces the conflict.

Common questions

Why can a page end up with two canonical tags?

Because more than one system on the page believes it owns the job. A common pairing: an SEO plugin (Yoast, RankMath, and similar) auto-generates a canonical tag from the page's own URL on every request, while a hand-written template -- left over from before the plugin was installed, or added by a developer who did not know the plugin already handled it -- emits its own canonical tag pointing at a different path. Neither system checks whether the other already added one.

Which canonical tag actually wins?

Browsers and search engines honor only the first <link rel="canonical"> tag found in the page's <head> and ignore every one after it. Which tag renders first depends on template output order -- something no one on the team necessarily controls or has looked at -- so the winner is effectively arbitrary from the page author's point of view, and can change silently the next time the template or plugin output order shifts.

Is two canonical tags worse than having none at all?

In one concrete sense, yes: with zero canonical tags, search engines infer a reasonable one on their own -- typically the URL you requested. With two conflicting ones, the page is actively telling crawlers two different things about itself, and which instruction wins is decided by markup order rather than intent. A missing canonical is a gap a search engine fills in sensibly; a contradicting pair is the page's own head disagreeing with itself.

How would I actually find this on a real page?

View-source or the Elements panel shows every tag in <head>, including duplicates, but only if you think to scroll past the first canonical tag and check for a second one -- most manual checks stop at the first match. This tool's CLI fetches the page, collects every <link rel="canonical"> tag in <head> rather than stopping at the first, and flags a danger finding the moment two of them name different URLs.
